reasons: Only the first three of twelve sections were visible, so the rest of the file was not reviewed.
The header says the code was verified by a dry run, but that run is not visible here.

terms.meaning: a value that stands for missing data, such as n/a or none
loading outside data into the system
a trial run that checks results without saving them

sections.name: File setup, PLACEHOLDERS
sections.title: Placeholder list and header rules
sections.what: Lists the placeholder strings that stand for missing data, and the three approved decisions in the header.
sections.why: The header says these decisions were approved and verified in a dry run.
sections.watch_out: Do not change the placeholder list or the decisions without running the dry run check again.

sections.name: asAbsent, isHttp
sections.title: Empty-value and web address checks
sections.what: Turns placeholder text into an empty value, and checks whether a value is a web address.
sections.why: Likely reason: the import needs to treat missing-data words as absent, and to know which values are links.
sections.watch_out: Values starting with not found or not applicable are also treated as absent, so a real sentence starting that way is dropped.

sections.name: hostOf, camel, lastDay, DateResolution, Q_END
sections.title: Host name, name casing, and date helpers
sections.what: Gets the host name from a web address, converts underscore names to camel case, finds the last day of a month, and defines the date resolution shape and the quarter end dates.
sections.why: These are shared helpers for turning Compass values into clean dates and names.
sections.watch_out: The quarter end dates are fixed text, so a change to the quarter rule must change them too.

sections.name: resolveDate (part 1)
sections.title: Turning loose dates into calendar dates
sections.what: Takes a date written in a loose form, such as a year and month, a quarter, a half-year, or a season, and turns it into a full calendar date. It also records whether the result is exact or an estimate and adds a plain note explaining the choice. Text it cannot read becomes an unresolved result.
sections.why: Likely reason: source reports write dates loosely, and the app needs one calendar date per field. The code comments refer to approved decisions, but the decisions themselves are not recorded in the code.

sections.name: resolveDate: if
sections.title: Handling month-and-day dates
sections.what: Finishes the date rules by reading names like June 2022 or May 2, 2022. A full day date is kept as exact, while a month and year is set to the last day of that month and marked approximate. If the month name or day is not valid, the value is treated as unresolved.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The approximate flag appears to exist so that users can see which dates are estimates.
sections.watch_out: Month-and-year values are set to the last day of the month, so anyone reading a date should check the approximate flag before trusting the day.

sections.name: parseSignedMonths
sections.title: Reading signed month counts
sections.what: Reads a number of months that may carry a plus or minus sign, such as +12 or -3, and rounds it to a whole number. Anything that is not a plain number returns nothing.
sections.why: The comment says an earlier version rejected the plus sign and silently dropped most of the gas schedule values, so this version accepts it.
sections.watch_out: A value that fails the pattern becomes empty without any warning, so missing schedule values should be checked against the source.

sections.name: parseCapacity
sections.title: Reading capacity in megawatts
sections.what: Reads a capacity that is written with an MW unit and returns the number, along with a short reason. A bare number with no unit is not converted, and free text is kept only as a note.
sections.why: The code deliberately refuses to guess the unit, so the unit must be written in the source for a capacity number to be used.
sections.watch_out: Commas are removed from the number before it is read, so a value written with a decimal comma in another language would be read incorrectly.

sections.name: normStatus
sections.title: Converting status text to lifecycle
sections.what: Turns a free-text project status into one fixed lifecycle label, such as operational, under construction, cancelled, or planning. It returns nothing when no clean match exists, for example for mothballed.
sections.why: The comment says mothballed has no clean target, so the code leaves it blank rather than inventing a label.
sections.watch_out: The checks run in a fixed order, so changing the order of the lines can change which label a status receives.

sections.name: parseLithiumCapacity
sections.title: Reading lithium capacity in kilotonnes
sections.what: Reads a lithium production amount that has a clear kilotonne or tonne unit and returns it in kilotonnes per year. Tonne values are divided by 1,000. Bare numbers and unclear text are not converted.
sections.why: The code's comments say only unambiguous units are parsed, so the mapping never guesses.
sections.watch_out: The code cannot tell whether a tonne figure is an annual rate, so a total over several years could be recorded as a yearly amount.

sections.name: LITHIUM_LEAVES
sections.title: Lithium sub-industry matching rules
sections.what: A checklist of word patterns that map a lithium project's asset description to one of six lithium categories, such as direct lithium extraction, hard rock mine, or solar evaporation pond. The first matching pattern wins.
sections.why: The comment names a six-category list, which keeps lithium projects sorted into a fixed set of groups.
sections.watch_out: The order of the list decides the answer, so a description that matches two patterns goes to whichever comes first. Words like chemical and refin are broad and could match unrelated text.

sections.name: lithiumSubIndustry
sections.title: Picking the lithium sub-industry
sections.what: Runs the checklist from top to bottom against an asset description and returns the first category that matches. If there is no description or no match, it returns nothing.
sections.why: The comment says a missing category is left blank rather than filled with a guess.
sections.watch_out: Blank results are expected for unmatched descriptions, so an empty field does not by itself mean the import failed.

sections.name: subIndustry
sections.title: Picking the general power sub-industry
sections.what: Assigns a power plant category, such as cogeneration, combined cycle, peaking or open cycle, or steam, based on keywords in the asset description. If a description names both combined and open cycle, or is too generic, it returns nothing.
sections.why: The comments say hybrid or vague descriptions are left blank on purpose, and the original text is kept as a separate attribute.
sections.watch_out: The keyword gas turbine is treated as open cycle, so a description that mentions a gas turbine without the word combined could be placed in the wrong category.

summary: Helper functions that clean up raw values from Compass flat files, turning placeholder text into empty values and checking web addresses.
purpose: Part of the import step that turns Compass data into the app's format.
why: The header says these functions were copied from a verified dry run, and must not change without running that check again.
how: Partly visible. It lists the placeholder strings and turns them into empty values, checks whether a value is a web address, and reads the host name from a URL. The date and capacity helpers are not visible in full.
inputs: Raw cell values from a Compass file.
outputs: Cleaned text or an empty value.
risks: Changing these helpers changes the imported data. Placeholders must match the list exactly, or they will be imported as text.
debug: If a value that has text shows as empty, check the placeholder list and the rule for values starting with not found. If a web address is rejected, check the address pattern.
